messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammed, a 55-year-old Middle Eastern man, has been a farmer for most of his life. Married and dedicated to his work, he finds solace in the routine of tending to his land. However, a traumatic assault several months ago has left him struggling with symptoms that have increasingly disrupted his daily life. On the night of the assault, Mohammed was working late on his farm when an intruder approached him from behind, causing a sharp pain as the assailant struck him. The attack was swift and unexpected, leaving Mohammed disoriented and shaken. In the chaos, he could only remember fragmented pieces of the event—moments of intense fear, the smell of sweat, and the relentless pounding of his heart. These disjointed memories often resurface during moments when he perceives a threat, such as when someone acts suspiciously near him. The somatic triggers, particularly the sensation of his own heart racing or the smell of sweat, have become powerful reminders of that night. When these sensations arise, Mohammed feels an overwhelming urge to ruminate on how to get even with the person who attacked him. This fixation on revenge consumes much of his mental energy, leading him to avoid dates and anniversaries connected to the event out of fear they might trigger painful memories. In his efforts to cope with the trauma, Mohammed has thrown himself into work as a way to keep his mind occupied. He often works late into the night, hoping that physical exhaustion will help dull the intruding thoughts. However, this overworking has taken a toll on both his health and relationships. His wife notices how he has become more withdrawn and distant, spending less time with her and more time working. The fragmented nature of his memories makes it difficult for Mohammed to fully process what happened. When he tries to explain the event, he often loses the thread and cannot finish recounting the details. This disconnect from his own experience leaves him feeling like an observer rather than a participant in his own life. Recently, these symptoms have intensified to the point where they are interfering with his ability to function effectively on the farm. The constant monitoring of perceived threats and the overwhelming urge for revenge have become burdensome. What frightens Mohammed most is the fear that he will continue to spiral downward if he does not find a way to regain control over his thoughts and emotions. What finally brought Mohammed to seek help was the realization that his preoccupation with revenge and avoidance strategies were affecting his relationships and his work. He hopes for a sense of closure and peace, wishing to reclaim his life from the grip of these haunting memories and triggers. His current state is one of deep concern and hope for finding effective ways to manage his symptoms and regain a semblance of normalcy in his daily life.
